title: Module Documentation: Erdos Problem #1053
content: Header documentation for Problem #1053: if sigma(n) = k*n (n is k-perfect), must k = o(log log n)? Summarizes the background on perfect, multiperfect, and k-perfect numbers for k up to 11, and states the problem is open (Guy's Problem B2).
mathContext: For $k$-perfect numbers ($\sigma(n) = kn$), is $k = o(\log \log n)$? Gronwall's theorem gives $\limsup \sigma(n)/(n \log \log n) = e^\gamma$, so $k = O(\log \log n)$ is the natural upper scale.

title: sigma: Sum-of-Divisors Function
content: Axiomatizes sigma(n) as a natural number. The sum-of-divisors function sigma(n) = sum_{d | n} d is one of the most fundamental arithmetic functions. It is multiplicative: sigma(mn) = sigma(m)*sigma(n) for coprime m, n. For prime powers, sigma(p^k) = (p^{k+1} - 1)/(p - 1).
mathContext: $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \mid n} d$. Multiplicative: $\sigma(p^a) = \frac{p^{a+1} - 1}{p - 1}$. For the problem: $\sigma(n) = kn$ means $n$ is $k$-perfect.

title: sigma_def: Linking to Mathlib
content: Axiomatizes that sigma(n) equals (Nat.divisors n).sum id for n > 0, connecting the axiomatized sigma to Mathlib's concrete divisor set. This ensures compatibility with Mathlib's number theory library.
mathContext: $\sigma(n) = \sum_{d \in \text{Nat.divisors}(n)} d$ for $n > 0$. Nat.divisors gives the finset $\{d \in \mathbb{N} : d \mid n\}$.

title: IsKPerfect: k-Perfect Number
content: Defines IsKPerfect(n, k) as n > 0 and sigma(n) = k*n. A positive integer n is k-perfect when its divisor sum is exactly k times n. For k=1, only n=1 qualifies. For k=2, these are the classical perfect numbers (6, 28, 496, ...). The concept generalizes to multiperfect numbers for k >= 3.
mathContext: $n$ is $k$-perfect if $n > 0$ and $\sigma(n) = kn$, equivalently $\sum_{d \mid n} d = kn$. The abundance $\sigma(n)/n - 1$ measures how far $n$ is from being perfect.

title: perfectMultiplicity: The Ratio sigma(n)/n
content: Defines perfectMultiplicity(n) = sigma(n)/n using natural number division. When n is k-perfect, perfectMultiplicity(n) = k. This ratio, also called the abundancy index, measures how 'perfect' a number is: it equals 2 for perfect numbers and grows toward e^gamma * log log n for highly composite numbers.
mathContext: The abundancy index $I(n) = \sigma(n)/n$. For $k$-perfect $n$: $I(n) = k$. Gronwall's theorem: $\limsup_{n \to \infty} I(n) / \log \log n = e^\gamma$.

title: one_perfect_unique: k=1 Uniqueness
content: Axiomatizes that only n=1 satisfies sigma(n) = n (1-perfect). Since sigma(n) >= n + 1 for all n >= 2 (as both 1 and n are divisors), 1 is the unique 1-perfect number.
mathContext: For $n \ge 2$: $\sigma(n) \ge 1 + n > n$, so $\sigma(n) = n$ only for $n = 1$.

title: perfect_examples: Classical Perfect Numbers
content: Axiomatizes that 6, 28, 496, and 8128 are 2-perfect. These are the first four perfect numbers, known since antiquity. sigma(6) = 1+2+3+6 = 12 = 2*6, sigma(28) = 1+2+4+7+14+28 = 56 = 2*28, etc. All correspond to Mersenne primes: 2^2-1=3, 2^3-1=7, 2^5-1=31, 2^7-1=127.

title: euler_even_perfect: Euclid-Euler Characterization
content: Axiomatizes Euler's theorem: an even number n is 2-perfect if and only if n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1) where 2^p - 1 is a Mersenne prime. This completely characterizes even perfect numbers. Combined with the unsolved odd perfect number problem, this shows perfect numbers are deeply connected to Mersenne primes.
mathContext: Euclid-Euler: Even $n$ is perfect $\iff n = 2^{p-1}(2^p - 1)$ with $2^p - 1$ prime. Currently 52 Mersenne primes are known, giving 52 known even perfect numbers.

title: triperfect_examples: k=3 Examples
content: Axiomatizes that 120, 672, and 523776 are 3-perfect (triperfect). Only six triperfect numbers are known in total: 120, 672, 523776, 459818240, 1476304896, 51001180160. No others have been found despite extensive computation, suggesting the list may be complete.
mathContext: $\sigma(120) = 360 = 3 \cdot 120$, $\sigma(672) = 2016 = 3 \cdot 672$, $\sigma(523776) = 1571328 = 3 \cdot 523776$. All six known triperfect numbers are even.

title: largest_known_k: k=11 Exists
content: Axiomatizes the existence of an 11-perfect number. The largest known k for which k-perfect numbers are known is k=11; these numbers have hundreds of digits. The question of whether k=12 examples exist is open. All known multiperfect numbers for k >= 3 are even.
mathContext: $\exists\, n: \sigma(n) = 11n$. The smallest known 11-perfect number has over 100 digits. For comparison, the smallest 5-perfect number is $14182439040$.

title: erdos_1053_conjecture: The Main Question
content: The central conjecture of Problem #1053: for any epsilon > 0, there exists N such that for all k-perfect n >= N, k < epsilon * log(log(n)). This formalizes k = o(log log n) using the standard epsilon-N definition of little-o. Robin's inequality gives the weaker O(log log n), but the strict o() bound is what Erdos asked.
mathContext: Erdős's conjecture: $\forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N,\; \forall n \ge N: \sigma(n) = kn \implies k < \varepsilon \log \log n$. Equivalently, if $(n_i, k_i)$ are $k_i$-perfect numbers with $n_i \to \infty$, then $k_i / \log \log n_i \to 0$.

title: gronwall_bound: Gronwall's Theorem (1913)
content: Axiomatizes Gronwall's fundamental theorem: for any epsilon > 0, sigma(n) <= (1+epsilon) * e^gamma * n * log log n for all sufficiently large n. The constant e^gamma ~ 1.781 is optimal: equality is approached along colossally abundant numbers. This establishes that sigma(n)/n = O(log log n).
mathContext: Gronwall (1913): $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{\sigma(n)}{n \log \log n} = e^\gamma \approx 1.7810724$, where $\gamma \approx 0.5772$ is the Euler-Mascheroni constant.

title: robin_inequality_conditional: Robin's Inequality (1984)
content: Axiomatizes Robin's inequality: sigma(n) < e^gamma * n * log log n for all n >= 5041, conditional on the Riemann Hypothesis. Robin proved that this inequality holds for all sufficiently large n if and only if RH is true, providing a remarkable connection between the sum-of-divisors function and the distribution of primes.
mathContext: Robin (1984): RH $\iff \sigma(n) < e^\gamma \cdot n \cdot \log \log n$ for all $n \ge 5041$. The exceptions below 5041 are superabundant numbers.

title: guy_finiteness_conjecture: Guy's Conjecture
content: Axiomatizes Guy's conjecture: for each k >= 3, the set of k-perfect numbers is finite (Set.Finite). This is strictly stronger than Erdos's o(log log n) question, since finiteness implies that eventually there are no k-perfect numbers at all for each fixed k >= 3. The conjecture is supported by extensive computation showing very few k-perfect numbers for each k.
mathContext: Guy's conjecture: For each $k \ge 3$, $|\{n : \sigma(n) = kn\}| < \infty$. If true, this implies Erdős's conjecture since $k$ is bounded for $k$-perfect $n \to \infty$.

title: robin_gives_O_bound: O(log log n) for k
content: Axiomatizes the consequence of Robin's inequality for k-perfect numbers: if n >= 5041 and sigma(n) = k*n, then k < e^gamma * log log n. This gives k = O(log log n) conditional on RH. The gap between this O() bound and the o() bound in Erdos's conjecture is the heart of Problem #1053.
mathContext: From Robin: $\sigma(n) < e^\gamma n \log \log n$ and $\sigma(n) = kn$ gives $k < e^\gamma \log \log n$. The question is whether the constant $e^\gamma$ can be replaced by any $\varepsilon \to 0$.
prerequisites: O(log log n) vs o(log log n)
